why_how.text: Indicators on your credential carry real decisions, such as an organ donation choice that family cannot override.
Each military indicator needs a specific document, so bringing the right one saves a second branch trip.

scenario.text: Zoe is sixteen and wants the donor heart on her first credential.

reasoning.text: A person under eighteen can declare the wish to donate only with a parent's or legal guardian's permission, and that adult must consent at death.

result.text: Zoe's mother gives permission, and the small heart is added to the front of Zoe's credential.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking family members can cancel an adult's organ donor choice after death.

correction.text: Under the Donor Choice Law, a person aged eighteen or older can declare the wish to donate, and family members cannot override it.

memory_support.text: Heart for donors; card, discharge or family papers for service.

prompt.text: A surviving spouse of a deceased veteran wants the veteran spouse indicator. Which documents are needed?

answer.text: Proof of the veteran's discharge or separation, the marriage certificate and the veteran's death certificate.

rationale.text: The spouse indicator needs all three documents, unlike the veteran indicator, which uses a DD two fourteen.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on indicators. Your Indiana credential can carry more than your name and photo. A small symbol can record that you have chosen to be an organ donor, and military indicators can show active-duty service, veteran status or that you are a surviving spouse of a veteran. Each indicator has its own rules about who can add it and what proof is needed. By the end of this lesson you will know how the donor choice works for adults and minors and which document backs each military indicator. Let us begin with the donor heart.

lines.text: Donor choice puts a heart on the front.
Minors need a parent or guardian.

narration.text: Choosing to be an organ donor puts a small heart on the front of your credential. Under Indiana's Donor Choice Law, a person aged eighteen or older can declare the wish to be an organ donor, and family members cannot override that choice at death. The rule is different for minors. A person under eighteen can declare the wish to donate only with a parent's or legal guardian's permission, and that adult must consent to donation when the minor dies. So an adult's declaration is binding on its own, while a minor's depends on the parent or guardian's consent.

lines.text: Active duty: current Common Access Card.

narration.text: An active-duty member of the US Armed Forces can add an active-duty indicator by showing a current Common Access Card at a branch during a new issuance or renewal. A veteran who was not dishonorably discharged can add a veteran indicator by providing a Department of Defense DD two fourteen that verifies the discharge. A surviving spouse of a deceased veteran can add a veteran spouse indicator by presenting proof of the veteran's discharge or separation, the marriage certificate and the veteran's death certificate. Match the document to the indicator before you go to the branch.

lines.text: Trap: family can undo an adult's choice.
Trap: one document fits every indicator.

narration.text: Here are two traps. First, many people believe relatives have the final word on organ donation. For an adult, they do not; the Donor Choice Law means family members cannot override an adult's declared wish. Only for a minor does a parent or guardian's consent decide the matter. Second, people assume any military paperwork will do. Each indicator has its own proof: a current Common Access Card for active duty, a DD two fourteen for a veteran, and discharge proof plus marriage and death certificates for a surviving spouse. Bring the document that matches.

Here is a quick check: the surviving spouse of a deceased veteran wants to add the veteran spouse indicator. Which documents must be presented? Think about what the BMV needs to confirm: that the veteran served and was discharged or separated, that the applicant was married to the veteran, and that the veteran has died. So the answer is proof of the veteran's discharge or separation, the marriage certificate and the veteran's death certificate. A DD two fourteen alone is the veteran's own route. If you named only one document, review the spouse indicator.

Let us wrap up. Choosing to be an organ donor adds a small heart to the front of your credential. Adults aged eighteen or older make a choice that family cannot override, while minors need a parent or guardian's permission, and that adult must consent at the time of death. For military indicators, active-duty members show a current Common Access Card at a new issuance or renewal, veterans who were not dishonorably discharged provide a DD two fourteen, and surviving spouses present discharge proof, the marriage certificate and the death certificate.

why_how.text: Your driver's license also matters on the water, because boats over ten horsepower require one or an approved boater course.
A license suspension and bad boating can follow you onto your driver record.
Where you live changes the boundary waters rule, so visitors and residents follow different license rules.

scenario.text: Sam is sixteen, has no driver's license, and wants to run his family's fifteen-horsepower boat.

reasoning.text: Without a license, a person fifteen or older may operate such a boat only after a DNR-approved boater education course and must carry a valid Indiana ID card.

result.text: Sam completes the approved boater course and carries his Indiana ID card when he takes the boat out.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a fourteen-year-old can run a boat over ten horsepower after taking a boater course.

correction.text: Nobody younger than fifteen may operate a watercraft with an engine of more than ten horsepower; the course route starts at fifteen.

memory_support.text: Ten horsepower needs a license, fifteen needs a course.

prompt.text: Lisa, an Illinois resident, takes her boat out on Indiana waters. On which waters does she need an Indiana driver's license?

answer.text: Only on an embayment, river or stream in Indiana.

rationale.text: Out-of-state residents need an Indiana license only on Indiana embayments, rivers or streams, while Indiana residents need one on boundary waters too.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on watercraft and your driver's license. It may seem odd, but the Indiana driver's manual includes rules for boats, because operating some watercraft requires a valid driver's license. You will learn where the horsepower line falls, how a person without a license can still operate a powered boat, who may never operate one, how a suspension and bad boating affect your driving record, and which license rules apply on Indiana's boundary waters for residents and for visitors from other states. Let us start with horsepower.

lines.text: Over ten horsepower: carry a license.

narration.text: Anyone operating a watercraft whose engine produces more than ten horsepower must carry a valid driver's license. There is a route for people without a license. A person aged fifteen or older may operate such a watercraft only after finishing a boater education course approved by the Indiana Department of Natural Resources, and must carry a valid Indiana ID card while doing so. Nobody younger than fifteen may operate a watercraft with an engine of more than ten horsepower at all. So the two numbers to remember are ten horsepower and fifteen years.

Your driving status follows you onto the water. A person whose driver's license is suspended may not operate a watercraft, and reckless or intoxicated boating or breaking watercraft laws can add points to the driver record. Location matters too. On Indiana boundary waters, Indiana residents operating a watercraft must carry an Indiana driver's license, while residents of other states need one only on an embayment, river or stream in Indiana. So an Indiana resident needs the license on boundary waters, and a visitor needs it on Indiana's inland waters.

lines.text: Trap: a course works at fourteen.
Trap: one rule for every boater.

narration.text: Here are two traps. First, the boater course does not open the door to younger teens. The course route applies only from age fifteen; nobody younger than fifteen may operate a watercraft with an engine over ten horsepower, course or not. Second, the boundary waters rule depends on where you live. Indiana residents must carry an Indiana license on boundary waters, but residents of other states need an Indiana license only on an embayment, river or stream in Indiana. Check the operator's age and home state before you answer a boating question.

Here is a quick check: Lisa lives in Illinois and boats on Indiana waters. Where must she carry an Indiana driver's license? Use the residency rule. Indiana residents must carry an Indiana license on boundary waters, but residents of other states need one only on an embayment, river or stream in Indiana. Lisa is an out-of-state resident, so she needs the Indiana license only on Indiana embayments, rivers or streams. Her boat's horsepower and her age still matter for the other rules. If you said every Indiana water, that rule is for Indiana residents.

Let us wrap up. Operating a watercraft whose engine produces more than ten horsepower requires carrying a valid driver's license. Without one, a person fifteen or older may operate such a boat after an approved boater education course while carrying a valid Indiana ID card, and nobody under fifteen may operate one at all. A suspended driver may not operate a watercraft, and reckless or intoxicated boating can add points. Indiana residents carry an Indiana license on boundary waters, while out-of-state residents need one only on Indiana embayments, rivers or streams.

why_how.text: A placard lets eligible people use reserved parking, so knowing who qualifies and how to apply matters to many families.
Placards expire on different schedules, and using an expired one can bring a fine.

scenario.text: Ray broke his leg, and his physician expects the injury to last four months.

reasoning.text: A temporary placard is available for a temporary disability, a provider completes the form, and the placard expires on the provider's stated date or after one year, whichever comes first.

result.text: Ray's physician completes the form, Ray pays the temporary placard fee, and the placard expires on the date his physician stated.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a valid placard lets you park in the diagonally striped area beside a reserved space.

correction.text: Parking in that striped area is never allowed, even with a valid placard.

memory_support.text: Permanent free, temporary a year, groups the fourth January.

prompt.text: Is a permanent disability parking placard free, and when does it expire?

answer.text: Yes, it is free, and it does not expire unless the disability or veteran status is certified to have changed.

rationale.text: A permanent placard is free and open-ended, unlike a temporary placard, which has a fee and lasts at most one year.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on disability parking placards. A placard allows eligible people to use parking reserved for drivers and passengers with disabilities. In this lesson you will learn who can get a placard, including people with disabilities, eligible veterans and certain organizations, how the application works, and how long each kind of placard lasts. You will also learn one parking rule that applies even when your placard is valid. These rules are practical for anyone who drives a family member with a disability, not only for placard holders.

A disability parking placard is available to people with a permanent or temporary disability, to people issued or eligible for a Disabled Hoosier Veteran plate, and to organizations providing transportation or facilities for people with physical disabilities. A company empowered by the state or a political subdivision to run such programs may also apply. To apply, a health care provider, such as a physician, chiropractor, podiatrist, physician's assistant, advanced practice registered nurse, optometrist or ophthalmologist, completes State Form forty-two zero seventy, which can be taken to any branch or mailed. Disabled Hoosier Veteran plate holders need no provider certification.

lines.text: Temporary: fee, at most one year.

narration.text: A permanent placard is free and does not expire unless a provider certifies the disability is no longer permanent, or the Indiana Department of Veteran Affairs certifies the holder is no longer a Disabled Hoosier Veteran. A temporary placard carries a fee and expires on the provider's stated date or one year after issue, whichever comes first. A placard issued to an organization expires on January first of the fourth year after the issue year, or earlier if the organization stops running programs or facilities for people with disabilities. Three placard types, three different lifetimes.

Holding a placard comes with rules of its own. Using an expired placard can lead to a fine, so keep an eye on the expiration date of a temporary or organization placard. The other rule applies even when your placard is valid. Parking in the diagonally striped area beside a reserved space is never allowed. That area is not an extra parking spot; it is kept clear beside the reserved space. So a valid placard lets you use the reserved space itself, but never the striped area next to it, and an expired placard should not be used at all.

lines.text: Temporary placards end within a year.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because a permanent placard is free and does not expire, people assume every placard works the same way. A temporary placard carries a fee and expires on the provider's stated date or one year after issue, whichever comes first. An organization's placard expires on January first of the fourth year after the issue year. And the second trap is the striped area. Even a valid placard never allows parking in the diagonally striped area beside a reserved space. When you answer a placard question, first decide which type of placard it is.

Here is a quick check: is a permanent disability parking placard free, and when does it expire? Recall the permanent placard rule. A permanent placard is free, and it does not expire unless a health care provider certifies that the disability is no longer permanent, or the Indiana Department of Veteran Affairs certifies the holder is no longer a Disabled Hoosier Veteran. So the answer is yes, it is free, and it has no set expiry. That is the opposite of a temporary placard, which has a fee and lasts at most a year. If you mixed them up, review the three placard types.

Let us wrap up. Placards are available to people with permanent or temporary disabilities, to people eligible for a Disabled Hoosier Veteran plate, and to qualifying organizations and state-empowered companies. A health care provider completes the state form, which goes to a branch or by mail, and Disabled Hoosier Veteran plate holders need no certification. Permanent placards are free with no set expiry, temporary placards cost a fee and last at most a year, and organization placards expire on January first of the fourth year. Expired placards can bring a fine, and the striped area is never for parking.

why_how.text: Renewing on time avoids the administrative penalty and, after long lapses, extra exams.
Renewal windows differ by credential and status, so knowing yours lets you renew early when that is allowed.

scenario.text: Dan's license expired six years ago, and he wants to drive again.

reasoning.text: A license expired five years or more needs the administrative penalty plus a knowledge exam, a driving skills exam and a vision screening.

result.text: Dan pays the penalty and passes the knowledge exam, the driving skills exam and the vision screening before his license is renewed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a credential expires on the anniversary of the day it was issued.

correction.text: All credentials except a probationary license expire at midnight on the holder's birthday.

memory_support.text: Birthday midnight, penalty if late, five years adds driving.

prompt.text: Carla let her license lapse two years ago and now wants to renew. What will she need?

answer.text: The administrative penalty, a knowledge exam and a standard vision screening.

rationale.text: Expired at least one hundred eighty days but not more than five years means the penalty, a knowledge exam and a vision screening, without the skills exam.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on expiration and renewal. Getting your license is only the beginning; you also have to keep it current. In this lesson you will learn when credentials expire, what happens when your birthday falls on a day branches are closed, who can renew online, how early you may renew, what renewing late costs and requires, how points can bring back the knowledge exam, and the special rules for people serving in the armed forces outside Indiana. Renewal questions are full of numbers, so pay close attention to each window.

lines.text: Probationary: twenty-one years and thirty days.

narration.text: A probationary license expires at twenty-one years and thirty days and may be renewed online if the holder qualifies, while all other credentials expire at midnight on the holder's birthday. If your birthday falls on a day when branches are closed, the credential expires at midnight on the next business day. Expiration dates differ for residents with temporary lawful status. If your name and residential address have not changed, you may be eligible to renew or replace online at myBMV.com, and online or kiosk renewal is allowed every other renewal. A person who loses a credential while temporarily outside Indiana may get an interim credential.

lines.text: One-eighty days to five years: knowledge and vision.
Five years or more: add driving.

narration.text: Everyone who renews a credential after its expiration date is subject to an administrative penalty. The testing depends on how long the license has been expired. Renewing a license expired for at least one hundred eighty days but not more than five years requires the administrative penalty, a knowledge exam and a standard vision screening. Renewing a license expired for five years or more requires the penalty plus a knowledge exam, a driving skills exam and a standard vision screening. So the longer the lapse, the more you must prove before you can drive again.

lines.text: Citizens and permanent residents: twenty-four months.

narration.text: You may also renew before expiration. US citizens and permanent lawful residents can renew a license or ID card up to twenty-four months before it expires, while people with lawful temporary status can renew only up to thirty days ahead. A learner's permit can be renewed up to thirty days before it expires. Those windows are very different, so check which group you are in. A citizen can take care of renewal up to two years in advance, but a permit holder or a lawful temporary resident must wait until the final thirty days before expiration.

lines.text: Twenty-one plus with six points: knowledge exam.
Service outside Indiana: valid ninety days after.

narration.text: A driver aged twenty-one or older with six or more active points must pass the knowledge exam to renew the license. Military service has its own rule. A license held by someone serving outside Indiana with the US Armed Forces stays valid for ninety days after discharge, post-deployment or the end of the out-of-state service residence. To renew an expired license after discharge, a veteran visits a branch with Department of Defense proof of discharge or the long form DD two fourteen, and can add the veteran indicator at that visit. Chauffeur license holders are pointed to the For-Hire Endorsement section of Chapter Two.

lines.text: Trap: everyone renews two years early.
Trap: five years adds only vision.

narration.text: Here are two traps. First, the twenty-four-month early renewal window belongs to US citizens and permanent lawful residents renewing a license or ID card. A learner's permit, or a credential held by someone with lawful temporary status, can be renewed only up to thirty days ahead. Second, the late-renewal tiers. A license expired from one hundred eighty days to five years needs the penalty, a knowledge exam and a vision screening; a license expired five years or more also needs a driving skills exam. Identify the group and the length of the lapse before answering.

Here is a quick check: Carla's license expired two years ago. What does renewing it require? Place her lapse in the right tier. A license expired at least one hundred eighty days but not more than five years needs the administrative penalty, a knowledge exam and a standard vision screening. Two years falls in that tier, so the answer is the penalty, a knowledge exam and a vision screening. She does not need the driving skills exam, which is added only for licenses expired five years or more. If you added the skills exam, review where the five-year line falls.

lines.text: Birthday midnight; closed day moves it.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. Most credentials expire at midnight on your birthday, a probationary license at twenty-one years and thirty days, and a closed-branch birthday moves expiry to the next business day. Online renewal is possible every other time if your name and address are unchanged. Renewing late brings a penalty, plus a knowledge exam and vision screening after one hundred eighty days, and a driving skills exam too after five years. Citizens renew up to twenty-four months early, permits and temporary residents thirty days. Six active points at twenty-one or older means the knowledge exam, and service members get ninety days after service.

why_how.text: After a move or a name change, the law gives you a deadline to amend your credential.
Knowing when a replacement can be ordered online saves a trip to the branch.

scenario.text: Ana moves to a new home in Indiana and changes only her mailing address online.

reasoning.text: A principal address change must be reported and an amended credential applied for within thirty days, in person at a branch with documents, while a mailing address can be changed online.

result.text: Ana also visits a branch with her documents within thirty days to update her principal address.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a mailing address update also changes your principal address.

correction.text: A principal address change needs a branch visit with documents within thirty days, while a mailing address change can be done online, at a kiosk or at a branch.

memory_support.text: Thirty days for a move or a name; Social Security first.

prompt.text: Pat legally changed her name. What must she do before going to the BMV?

answer.text: Update her Social Security records and wait at least one business day.

rationale.text: The name change order is Social Security first, a wait of at least one business day, then a branch visit within thirty days.

narration.text: Welcome to the lesson on amendments and replacements. Life changes, and your credential has to keep up. In this lesson you will learn what to do after a legal change to your personal information, the deadline for reporting a new home address, how a mailing address change differs, the order of steps for a name change, and when you can replace a lost or stolen card online. These are procedures rather than road rules, but they come with firm deadlines, and missing one can leave you with a credential that does not match your records.

lines.text: Legal change: amend at any branch.
Principal address: thirty days, in person.
Mailing address: online, kiosk or branch.

narration.text: After legally changing personal information you must amend your credential, which can be done at any BMV branch. A change of principal, or legal, address must be reported and an amended credential applied for within thirty days, in person at a branch with Appendix A documents. A mailing address is different. It can be changed online at myBMV.com, at a BMV Connect kiosk or at a branch. So the principal address, where you legally live, has a thirty-day in-person deadline, while the mailing address, where your post arrives, can be updated from home.

lines.text: Wait at least one business day.

narration.text: For a name change, the order of steps matters. First update your Social Security records, then wait at least one business day, then visit a branch within thirty days of the change with Appendix A documents to amend the credential. Doing it in the wrong order can stall the amendment, because your legal name must match Social Security records. The manual also notes that if your Indiana license, permit or ID card is not expired, the SSA card replacement can be done online at no cost. Plan the Social Security step first and the branch visit second.

lines.text: Other changes: branch within thirty days.

narration.text: A lost or stolen credential can be replaced through myBMV.com or a BMV Connect kiosk when your name and residential address are unchanged. Online replacement is capped at ten times, after which you must replace the credential at a BMV branch. If anything other than the mailing address has changed, a replacement cannot be ordered online; you must amend the credential at a branch within thirty days with Appendix A documents. So the online route is for simple replacements where nothing important has changed, and the branch handles everything else.

lines.text: Principal address needs a branch visit.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Updating your mailing address online feels like updating your address, full stop. It is not. The principal address, your legal residence, must be reported and amended within thirty days, in person at a branch with documents. A mailing address change can be made online, at a kiosk or at a branch, but it does not replace the principal address update. The same thinking applies to replacements: if anything other than the mailing address has changed, you cannot order a replacement online. Ask which address or detail changed before choosing the route.

Here is a quick check: Pat has legally changed her name. What must she do before going to the BMV? Recall the order of steps. For a name change, you update your Social Security records first, then wait at least one business day, then visit a branch within thirty days of the change with your Appendix A documents. So the answer is to update Social Security records and wait at least one business day. Going to the BMV first would put the steps out of order. If you said to start at the branch, review the name-change sequence.

lines.text: Thirty days for address or name.
Online only when details are unchanged.

narration.text: Let us wrap up. After a legal change to your personal information you amend your credential at any branch. A new principal address must be reported within thirty days in person with documents, while a mailing address can be changed online, at a kiosk or at a branch. For a name change, update Social Security first, wait a business day, then amend at a branch within thirty days. A lost or stolen card can be replaced online or at a kiosk when name and address are unchanged, up to ten times, and any other change means a branch visit within thirty days.
